tier_reason: The poisson2d/README.md table matches the record exactly (optimized Fortran 0.18 / 6.25 / 31.4 s against optimized C 0.37 / 6.80 / 32.8 s), and the code (optimized.c, optimized.f90), flags (-Ofast on both sides) and CPU (Ryzen 5 3600 under WSL2) are public. It is not A: neither the gcc nor the gfortran version is stated (the vibrato precedent), and the timed Fortran code was changed afterwards by PR #30 (2022-03-05), which fixed single-precision literals; under the later-fixed-code rule that caps it at C. The suite is the Fortran community's own one-person benchmark with one run per cell, so it is not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README timings (seconds, one run per cell, measured June 2021): optimized Fortran 0.18 / 6.25 / 31.4 against optimized C 0.37 / 6.80 / 32.8 for M=100 / 200 / 300. That is about 1.09x faster at M=200 and 1.04x at M=300 (derived from page data). The README says the M=100 C runs did nearly double the iterations, so that column is not comparable. The naive versions go the other way: naive Fortran 0.34 / 13.2 / 69.7 against naive C 0.42 / 7.25 / 33.7, so naive C is about 1.8-2.1x faster at M=200 and 300 (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: The margin is 4-9% on one machine, with a single run per cell under WSL2, and holds only for the hand-optimized pair (rho precomputed into an array, one copy per iteration). In the naive pair, naive C is about twice as fast as naive Fortran, so there is no consistent language-level win. (1) The timings predate PR #30 (Euler-37, merged 2022-03-05, titled 'change the precision problems in fortran files'). That PR changed a=0.01 to a=0.01_dp and y<0.8 to y<0.8_dp in both naive.f90 and optimized.f90. The timed Fortran therefore used a single-precision grid spacing (about 0.0099999998) and charge bound, and solved a slightly different problem from the C code; nobody re-timed after the fix. (2) The two programs do not solve the same instance even after the fix. C fills rhoa[i][j]=rho(i*a,j*a) with 0-based i, while Fortran fills rhoarr(i,j)=rho(i*a,j*a) with 1-based i, so the charge squares sit one cell apart relative to the grounded boundary and the iteration counts differ. The README gives no iteration counts, only 'approximately the same' for M=200/300 and 'nearly double' for C at M=100. A Discourse reply seen only as a search snippet reported about 320k Fortran against 304k C iterations on a 250x250 grid in an earlier version. A 4-9% margin is within that spread. (3) The C side keeps phi, phip and rhoa in malloc'd pointer-to-array buffers and passes them to out-of-line mmax/swap helpers without restrict. The Fortran side uses static arrays with whole-array assignment and maxval(abs()). A Discourse reply (snippet only) says the C code ran a few seconds slower with heap-allocated arrays. The gap is therefore at least partly a storage choice that C could also make, not a language property. (4) The Fortran loops run i outer and j inner over phiprime(i,j), which is stride-M access in column-major order. Any Fortran win therefore depends on gfortran interchanging the loops (-floop-interchange is part of -O3/-Ofast in GCC 8+), which was not verified. (5) The gcc and gfortran versions are not stated, the last commit is March 2022, and -Ofast enables -ffast-math on both sides. Timing uses clock() in C and cpu_time in Fortran, over the whole run in both. The linked Discourse thread (fortran-lang.discourse.group/t/performance-c-vs-fortran/1461) does not resolve here (ENOTFOUND); what it says was read from search snippets only.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the README. From the sources: the C baseline uses malloc'd, possibly aliasing pointer-to-array buffers passed without restrict to out-of-line helpers, while Fortran uses static arrays with whole-array copy and maxval. A Discourse reply (search snippet only) says the C code was slower with heap allocation. The edge therefore looks like an array-storage and aliasing difference within a few percent, possibly helped by slightly different iteration counts, not a codegen advantage of Fortran.

notes: Numbers verified on the README and all four sources read. Tier C stands (no compiler versions; the timed Fortran was later fixed for single-precision literals by PR #30), and the record is metadata-accurate (MIT, 26 stars, 10 forks, last commit 2022-03-05, abandoned). Shortcomings to record: 4-9% margin from a single run, inside the iteration-count spread; C and Fortran charge grids are offset by one cell; C baseline uses malloc'd buffers without restrict; Fortran loop order is cache-strided unless interchanged; naive C beats naive Fortran by about 2x; timings predate the PR #30 precision fix. Not a duplicate of the plb2 Fortran matmul entry (a different benchmark and suite).
